title: Dhul-Qarnayn's wall
hookLine: a just king builds a barrier of iron and copper for a people and calls it a mercy (18:83–98)

cards: The last story in al-Kahf starts with a question people put to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: tell us about Dhul-Qarnayn.
The name means the one with two horns, or the man of two ages, or of two ends of the earth; the commentators offer several. He's a ruler given power and the means to use it.
He travels to where the sun sets, then to where it rises, and then to a pass between two mountains, where a frightened people wait for him.

teach.h: GOG AND MAGOG AT THE PASS.
teach.b: The people at the pass, the surah says, could hardly understand speech. But they manage to say it: Ya'juj and Ma'juj, Gog and Magog, are ruining the land. Will you build a barrier between us and them if we pay you?
Dhul-Qarnayn turns the money down. What my Lord has given me is better, he says.

teach.h: NO PAYMENT. HELP ME WITH STRENGTH.
teach.b: Help me with your strength instead. Bring me blocks of iron. They stack the iron until it fills the gap between the mountainsides.
Then: blow, and they work the bellows until the iron glows like fire. Then: bring me molten copper to pour over it. The wall holds; the raiders could neither climb it nor dig through it.
Now the line this day is built on. Standing before what he built, he says, in Pickthall's words: "This is a mercy from my Lord".
And: when my Lord's promise comes, He will level it to the ground, and my Lord's promise is true. Earlier in this surah, a man walked through his gardens saying this will never perish.

teach.h: IT WILL FALL WHEN GOD DECIDES.
teach.b: Here a man stands before iron and copper and says: it's a mercy, and it will fall when God decides. Who was Dhul-Qarnayn?

teach.h: THIS IS A MERCY FROM MY LORD.
teach.b: Muslim scholars have long disagreed: some said Alexander the Great, some Cyrus of Persia, some an ancient king of Yemen. The Qur'an doesn't say.
It tells what he did with power: he refused payment, put people to work on their own protection, and gave the credit away.
In the modern four-trials reading, that completes the set: faith in the cave, wealth in the garden, knowledge by the sea, and power at the wall.

how: Muslims read the story of Dhul-Qarnayn as a model of just rule: power used to protect the weak, without payment, and credited to God; scholars have long debated his identity without agreement.

o: iron and copper across a pass, called a mercy
the wall al-Khidr rebuilt over an orphans' treasure
a stone wall the sleepers built at the cave

games.q: inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the one with two horns, or two ages

s: the Qur'an says Dhul-Qarnayn was Alexander the Great
it never names him; scholars have suggested Alexander, Cyrus, a king of Yemen and others.
he asked the people to help build the wall
he refused their money and asked for their strength.
he says the wall will stand forever
he calls it a mercy, and says God will level it when His promise comes.

games.q: a frightened people offer you payment to build a barrier against raiders. you're a ruler with means. what does Dhul-Qarnayn do?
o: refuse the money and ask for their strength.
tell them to build it themselves.
games.why: what my Lord has given me is better, he says. help me with strength. then they build it together.

practice: Bring to mind someone who needs protecting, a child, an aging parent, a coworker being worn down, yourself, and the gap their trouble gets in through.
Picture one small barrier you could help build with them, not for them: a bedtime, a budget, a boundary, a lock that works. And picture handing the credit away when it holds.

wordCard.voice: Dhul-Qarnayn's wall. Iron and molten copper across a mountain pass, built with the people's own hands, and called a mercy from God. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the one with two horns (qarn: horn, also an age or generation).

carryVoice: Your line: a mercy from my lord. Built with strength, credited to God. Day four hundred seventy.

sources.q: This is a mercy from my Lord
